title: The Scots Musical Museum
alternative_titles: The Scots Musical Museum, in Six Volumes
description: The great serial anthology of Scottish song, projected and published by the Edinburgh music-engraver James Johnson and issued in six volumes between 1787 and 1803. It prints traditional and modern Scots songs with their airs, arranged for the voice with simple instrumental accompaniments, and in its later volumes it became the principal printing ground for the songs of Robert Burns, who from about 1788 was its most active contributor and, in effect, its literary editor. The collection is the single most important body of song into which Burns poured his late labour: he revised old texts, recovered fragments from singers and from the printed repertoire, wrote new verses to familiar airs, and supplied the illustrative notes and the historical and critical remarks that carry the volumes. Its six volumes hold the repertory out of which the modern idea of the Scottish song tradition was made, and they document a collaboration between a music publisher and a poet in which the poet's share came to dominate the series.
plot_or_argument: The volumes are not a narrative but a repertory: each number is a song text printed with its air, arranged so that the words and the tune are presented together, with the older traditional pieces beside new or revised lyrics. The scheme broadens from the opening volume's gathering of favourite Scottish songs toward the later volumes' wider historical and comparative range, which includes early pieces, songs in the Scottish dialect, and illustrative prose notes on the texts and their authorities. Burns's contributions fall chiefly in the volumes issued from about 1790 onwards: songs of love, drinking and friendship, comic and pastoral songs, Jacobite and border pieces, and revised versions of traditional texts whose phrasing he restored or re-made. His own account of the work, in letters of the period, describes his method of collating printed and sung versions, keeping the old words where they were best, and writing new stanzas only when the air required them.
narrative_structure: A serial anthology in six octavo volumes, each a numbered sequence of independent songs rather than an ordered argument; the unity is the repertory and the continuing editorial scheme, which passed in practice from Johnson's musical arrangements to Burns's textual judgement as the series reached its middle volumes. The set was completed only after Burns's death, and he interleaved copies of the earlier volumes with his own notes and corrections.
principal_characters: the singer-speakers of the songs; the beloveds and false lovers of the lyric texts; the shepherd, hind and ploughboy of the pastoral and labouring numbers; the drunkards and revellers of the tavern songs; the Highland chiefs, border raiders and Jacobites of the historical pieces; James Johnson as projector and publisher and Robert Burns as contributing editor
literary_form: Anthology, reliques and editorial collection of Scottish song; ballad and popular song, printed with the airs and a vocal part
meter_and_prosody: Strophic song verse written to be sung, not read: the texts run mainly in the ballad and song stanzas of the Scottish repertory, common and short measure with alternating four- and three-beat lines, with refrains, tags and the short-tailed stanza forms Burns adapted to individual airs. Because the air governs the line, the metre is disciplined by musical phrase, syncopation and repeat, and Burns's revisions are often measurable as adjustments of syllable count to the notes. Scots dialect spelling, with its own rhyme and assonance habits, carries much of the series' verbal texture.
historical_context: Published at Edinburgh by James Johnson, engraver and music-seller, in the same decade as the Kilmarnock and Edinburgh volumes of Burns's poetry, the Museum belonged to the enthusiastic collecting of national song that followed Percy's Reliques and the ballad revivals of the 1780s, and to Edinburgh's competitive music trade, in which Johnson and his rival George Thomson vied for airs, verses and subscribers. Burns, established as a poet after 1786 and settled at Ellisland and then Dumfries from 1788, took up the collection as the work of his later years, believing that the old Scottish songs were a national inheritance worth preserving against the polite dilution of the English stage. His engagement made the series a partnership of a craftsman publisher and a poet-editor; the sixth volume appeared after his death in 1796.
literary_significance: The Museum is the repository in which Burns's achievement as a songwriter, the largest and most durable part of his work, was first collected and printed, and it changed the status of song within his canon from occasional verse to serious poetic labour. It also fixes the model of the poet at work on traditional texts, revising, restoring and re-creating rather than inventing, a model that bears directly on later accounts of Romantic authorship, orality and cultural property. Its repertory, edited and largely made by Burns, remains the standard record of late-eighteenth-century Scottish song and a central document of the Romantic construction of national tradition.
attribution_notes: The volumes are Johnson's publication and a joint undertaking: Johnson chose and engraved the airs, contracted the arrangements and holds the title-page credit, while Burns supplied an immense body of lyrics, revisions and notes without ever appearing as author of the work. Burns is named here as a contributing author only, not as the author of the collection. Estimates of his share run in modern accounts to some two hundred songs, but the figure varies between authorities and the attribution of individual numbers between traditional texts, other contributors and Burns has been actively re-opened by recent scholarship, so the record is left at research_status partial.
bibliographical_notes: First published at Edinburgh by James Johnson, engraver, who is also named on the imprints as Johnson and Johnson & Co.; six volumes, 1787-1803, octavo. The copy described here is the National Library of Scotland digitised set, catalogued as by James Johnson, 6 volumes, Edinburgh, printed and sold by Johnson & Co., 1787-1803; a facsimile reprint with Donald A. Low's introduction was issued by the Scolar Press in 1991. Burns's song work for the Museum is now edited in the Oxford University Press Collected Works of Robert Burns planned by the University of Glasgow Burns project.

title: A Select Collection of Original Scottish Airs for the Voice
alternative_titles: A Select Collection of Original Scotish Airs for the Voice
Select Collection of Original Scottish Airs
description: George Thomson's rival song collection, issued in five volumes from 1793 to 1818 and marketed as a polite as well as a national repertory: Scottish airs furnished with instrumental introductions and closings and with keyboard and string accompaniments written or adapted by Ignaz Pleyel, Leopold Koželuch and Joseph Haydn, and supplied with characteristic verses in Scots and, for the English market, with added English translations of the songs. Thomson, an Edinburgh writer to the signet and collector of music, made the series a commercial enterprise on a larger scale than James Johnson's Scots Musical Museum, and from 1793 he secured the labour of Robert Burns, whose songs and revisions for it were advertised on the title pages themselves as upwards of one hundred new songs. The collection is the scene of Burns's most sustained quarrel with an editor: Thomson wanted the dialect smoothed and the airs dressed for drawing-room sale, Burns insisted on the old words and on the singable economy of the stanza, and the resulting letters form the most systematic body of Romantic criticism of song-making.
plot_or_argument: As a repertory the work presents air after air with its text and its arrangement: Scottish melodies, many traditional, set with symphonies and accompaniments in the current keyboard style and fitted with verses in the Scottish dialect together with English rendering. The songs gathered or commissioned by Thomson cover love, absence and fidelity, drinking and fellowship, landscape and the rural round, and patriotic and border themes; Burns supplied new lyrics, restored or trimmed traditional texts, and proposed alternatives where he judged the existing words unworthy of the air. His correspondence with Thomson states the poetics behind the entries: that the poet must be the servant of the music, that old songs should be preserved with their imperfections, and that a single offending word can spoil a stanza sung to a favourite tune.
narrative_structure: A serial publication in five volumes of independent songs with musical settings, ordered by Thomson's commercial and musical scheme rather than by any argument; the volumes were issued successively between 1793 and 1818 with variant Edinburgh and London imprints, and the Burns material belongs chiefly to the numbers published during and just after his lifetime, the later volumes continuing without him.
principal_characters: the lovers, absent friends and false hearts of the song texts; the shepherds, reapers and harvest figures of the pastoral numbers; the honest drunkards and vagrants of the comic songs; George Thomson as editor-proprietor, Robert Burns as supplying poet, and the arrangers Pleyel, Koželuch and Haydn as the collection's other makers
literary_form: Anthology, reliques and editorial collection of Scottish song with musical arrangements; ballad and popular song written for publication in a polite album series
meter_and_prosody: Song stanzas measured to pre-existing airs, so that line length, stanza shape and refrain are dictated by the musical period; Burns's texts for Thomson move between common and short measure ballad stanzas, four-line and six-line song stanzas with tags, and the irregular stanzaic patterns he adopted for particular airs. The accompanying prose notes and letters show the working principle: syllable for syllable fitting to the notes, with elision in the Scots dialect used to keep the singer's phrase intact.
historical_context: Thomson's series appeared in the competitive Edinburgh music trade of the 1790s and after, when the demand for national airs among Scottish and English subscribers supported a cottage industry of collection, arrangement and subscription publishing. The first volumes relied on Pleyel and Koželuch; from the end of the century Haydn was engaged to arrange Scottish songs, which set the collection at the centre of a transnational exchange between Viennese classicism and Scottish tradition. Burns, who had known Thomson since the Edinburgh years of 1787, agreed in 1793 to supply verses; his contributions continued until his death in 1796, and the later volumes, with their added English verses, realised Thomson's programme of making Scots song saleable to a polite and English-speaking market.
literary_significance: The collection preserves the second and more commercially ambitious half of Burns's late song work, and its title-page claim to Burns's new songs made the poet's labour for a music publisher a public feature of the book. The Burns-Thomson correspondence called out by it is the chief Romantic document on the making of songs, on the authority of the tune over the text, and on the editorial handling of a national vernacular repertory. As a publishing object the series is the standard test case for the argument that the Romantic ballad revival was as much a commercial and musical enterprise as a literary one.
attribution_notes: This is Thomson's publication and Thomson's editorial conception, with musical arrangements by Pleyel, Koželuch and Haydn and verses by several hands; Robert Burns is not its author. Burns is named here only as the contributing poet whose songs the volumes advertise and whose dialect verses Thomson revised or replaced. The number of his contributions is variously stated in the scholarship (around one hundred songs is the common estimate, and the contemporary title pages claim upwards of one hundred new songs), and individual songs exist in more than one state because of Thomson's editorial interference, so each attribution within the series must be checked against the scholarly edition of Burns's songs for Thomson rather than taken from the printed volumes alone.
bibliographical_notes: Published by George Thomson, Edinburgh, with London sale also by Preston, in five volumes, 1793-1818; copies show variant imprints, including issues printed and sold by T. Preston and issues sold by the proprietor G. Thomson, and title pages advertising arrangements by Pleyel, Koželuch and Haydn and, in the numbers of 1800 and 1801, the greater number of the verses written for the work by Burns. Thomson's song publishing continued in later series into the 1840s; Burns's share is edited in the Glasgow and Oxford edition of his songs for Thomson.

title: The Columbiad
description: Barlow's national epic of the American republic, first published at Philadelphia in 1807 and re-modelled and enlarged in the text he issued in 1809, where the poem runs to ten books each preceded by a prose Argument. It is a recasting of his own earlier Vision of Columbus (1787) - the Preface calls that volume a sketch of the present poem - and it keeps the vision-frame of the older work while making it the vehicle of a far more ambitious historical argument. Christopher Columbus, chained and deserted in a Spanish prison after his final ruin, is visited by Hesper, the guardian genius of the western continent, and carried to a mount of vision above the coast of Spain; from there the poet and his guide survey, in order, the American continent and its peoples, the Inca empire of Capac and Oella, the destruction of Peru, the effect of the discovery upon Europe, the planting of the North American colonies, the war of Independence, and at last the future progress of the arts, of republican government, and of a general congress of nations. The poem is openly didactic: its declared object is to strengthen in the rising generation a sense of the importance of republican institutions, and it invokes Freedom rather than a Muse.
plot_or_argument: The Argument of Book I sets the frame: the condition of Columbus in a Spanish prison, his monologue on the great actions of his life and the manner in which they had been rewarded, the appearance and speech of Hesper, and the ascent of the mount of vision, whence Europe settles from their sight and America is described in its mountains, rivers, lakes, soil and productions. Book II shows the natives of America in vision, discusses the diversity of human beings and the first peopling of the continent, and passes to Mexico and its destruction by Cortez and to Cusco and Quito, with the tradition and the real history of Capac and Oella, founders of the Peruvian empire. Book III is the Inca narrative: the invasion of the mountain savages, the embassy of Rocha, the worshippers of the volcano and of the storm, the chief Zamor, the sacrifice of Rocha's companions and the death song of Azonto, the war dance, the rout of the Peruvians at an eclipse of the sun, and the recovery of Rocha. Book IV foretells the destruction of Peru, consoles Columbus with a vision of future ages, surveys the effect of the discovery on the commerce, government and letters of Europe, with the Jesuits, persecution and the Inquisition, then turns to Raleigh's plan for North America, the formation of the coast by the gulf stream, the first colonial settlements, the arrival of Delaware with settlers for Virginia, and the prophetic speech of Potowmak to the night scene on the Chesapeake. Books V to VII carry the American Revolution in vision: the colonies and their wars with France, Braddock's defeat and Washington, Bunker Hill and the death of Warren, Montgomery before Quebec, the treatment of American prisoners and the prison ship, the recrossing of the Delaware, Burgoyne's advance and the battles of Saratoga with the story of Lucinda, the alliance with France, Monmouth, Wayne's storming of Stonypoint, the fall of Charleston, Greene and Eutaw, the siege of York and Gloster and the capture of Cornwallis. Book VIII opens with a Hymn to Peace and an eulogy on the heroes slain, in which the author names his own brother; Atlas, the guardian genius of Africa, denounces to Hesper the crimes of his people in the slavery of the Africans, and the poet addresses his countrymen on that subject and on the principles of their government before the arts, fisheries, commerce and education of the United States are displayed. Book IX reasons from the progress of the physical world to the progress of the moral, answers Columbus's doubts with the rise of modern science - Copernicus, Kepler, Galileo, Newton, Bacon, Herschel, the printing press and the magnetic needle - and proposes the federal system extended over the whole earth. Book X resumes the vision over the whole world, foresees the assimilation and final union of languages and closes on a general congress from all nations assembled to establish the political harmony of mankind.
narrative_structure: A long didactic epic in ten books (in the 1809 recension, each book preceded by a prose Argument that summarises it) and unified not by a single action but by a sustained vision-frame: the dungeon and the mount of vision hold the narrative together while the panorama moves historically from geography to Inca romance to colonial settlement to revolutionary war to philosophical forecast. Time is deliberately manipulated - in Book VIII Hesper reverses the order of time to show the continent again in its savage state and so exhibit the progress of the arts - and the poem's parts are rhetorical set pieces (invocation, hymn, eulogy, denunciation, prophecy) rather than a plot.
principal_characters: Christopher Columbus; Hesper, the guardian genius of the western continent; Atlas, the guardian genius of Africa, who denounces the slavery of his people; Freedom, invoked in place of a Muse; Capac and Oella, founders of the Peruvian empire; Rocha, the Inca's son, and Azonto and Zamor of the savage armies; Raleigh and Delaware and the patriarchal settlers of Virginia; the river gods of the Chesapeake and Potowmak; Cortez; Washington, Warren and Montgomery; Lucinda, the heroine of the Saratoga episode
literary_form: National epic and didactic poem: a republican epic of discovery, settlement and progress built on a vision-frame, with prose arguments, hymn, eulogy and prophetic address
meter_and_prosody: Written in heroic couplets of closed decasyllabic rhyming pairs, the diction public, sententious and expository, with the couplet used for maxim and antithesis ("Almighty Freedom! give my venturous song / The force, the charm that to thy voice belong"). The Preface defends the choice of modern rather than classical subject matter and vocabulary, arguing that the names of modern weapons, machines and institutions are at least as poetical as the ancient ones, and expressly declines to prove that he has written an epic poem in the regular form, because the recentness and importance of his events would have debased them in a conventional modelling. The prose Arguments and the substantial prose notes on the historical and scientific passages make the verse part of an explicitly instructional apparatus.
historical_context: The poem belongs to the early republic's demand for a national literature and to Barlow's own career as poet, diplomat and republican controversialist: the first edition was published at Philadelphia in 1807, printed - as the Library of Congress catalogue records - at the expense of Robert Fulton, the steamboat engineer whose partner and friend Barlow had become, and with a portrait of the author and plates by Smirke. It grew out of The Vision of Columbus, a poem in nine books printed at Hartford in 1787 for the author, which had already made Columbus the subject of American verse; the 1807 text recast that poem as a national epic and the 1809 text re-modelled it again into ten books. Editions followed immediately in London (R. Phillips, 1809) and Paris (1813, with the last corrections of the author), and a Georgetown edition in 1825. Its publication revived the old quarrel over whether a republic could have an epic: critical observations on the poem were printed at Philadelphia in 1809, the abbé Grégoire addressed a letter to the author on the work, and Barlow's reply and a collected correspondence on the poem appeared in print in 1809 and 1810. A copy belonged to Thomas Jefferson's library, catalogued at Monticello.
literary_significance: The Columbiad is the most ambitious single attempt of the early American Republic to produce a national epic, and the document in which the revolutionary hope of the 1790s is re-stated as a philosophy of historical progress and continental destiny; its ten-book plan makes the discovery of America, the war of Independence and the projected congress of nations a single providence of reason, and its Book VIII puts the denunciation of African slavery into the machinery of the poem itself. Because Barlow revised his own earlier Vision of Columbus into it, the poem is also a case study in the transmission of revolutionary writing into the nineteenth century, and the surrounding pamphlet warfare of 1809-1810 is one of the fullest records of early American poetical criticism. It has long been slighted as the type of the ambitious failure, which is itself part of its significance: later accounts of American verse defined their own modernity against it.
attribution_notes: Single authorship is certain and the title page names the author. The record's bibliographical difficulty is not authorship but recension: the poem exists in materially different states - the Hartford 1787 Vision of Columbus as originally conceived, the 1807 recasting as The Columbiad, and the enlarged and re-modelled ten-book text of 1809, with further authorial correction in the 1813 Paris edition - so description and quotation in this record are tied to the 1809 text, which was consulted directly, while the publication date records the first edition of 1807. The Library of Congress catalogue note describes the 1807 volume as an amplification of the Vision of Columbus and Barlow's own Preface calls the earlier poem a sketch of the present work.
bibliographical_notes: First edition: Philadelphia, C. and A. Conrad, 1807, 8vo, 454 pp. with index (Library of Congress MARC record via the Open Library catalogue, which notes that the volume was printed at the expense of Robert Fulton and carries a portrait of Barlow and plates by Smirke). Second Philadelphia issue, 1809: published by C. and A. Conrad and Co., Philadelphia, and Conrad, Lucas and Co., Baltimore, Fry and Kammerer being the printers; a London edition of the same year was printed for R. Phillips (428 pp.), and an 1813 Paris edition for F. Schoell is entitled with the last corrections of the author. The text consulted for this record is the 1809 ten-book edition with prose Arguments, whose books I to X, invocation to Freedom and Arguments were verified in full.

title: The Hasty-Pudding
alternative_titles: The Hasty-Pudding: A Poem, in Three Cantos
description: Barlow's mock-heroic poem on a New England dish, three cantos of couplets written in exile at Chambéry in Savoy in January 1793 and first printed in 1796. Its premise is a burlesque of the epic and didactic conventions Barlow himself had used in the Columbiad material: the poet refuses his Alpine and revolutionary subject matter - the audacious Alps that cramp the day, the Gallic flags that bear death to kings and freedom to the world - and chooses instead a virgin theme, unconscious of the Muse, the sweets of Hasty-Pudding. The poem then treats cornmeal pudding with all the apparatus of serious verse: an invocation, a search for the dish's lineage through the wrecks of time, an origin myth in which a nameless Indian squaw, a tawny Ceres, first cracked the dried maize, sifted the golden flour and stirred it in boiling water, and a celebration of the pudding's appearance in the author's path of exile. Behind the joke is a political and cultural argument about diet, plainness and luxury: the Yankee's simple abundant feast that cheers servant and lord alike against the vicious rules of art of the French kitchen, the cities of Europe that exclude maize from their climes, and a footnote, appended to the passage on London lost in smoke and steeped in tea, in which Barlow names a certain king who was publishing proclamations to prevent American principles from being propagated in his country.
plot_or_argument: Canto I is invocation and origin: after rejecting the Alps and the Gallic flags the poet addresses the bowl directly, welcomes the milk smoking from the kine that tempers its heat, and asks what lovely squaw in days of yore first gave the food to the world, crediting some tawny Ceres with the invention of cracking the maize, sifting it through the rough seive and stirring the yellow flour till it swells, thickens, puffs and wallops to its true consistence. He claims the discovery of Oella, the Peruvian heroine of his own earlier poem, for the honour, then greets his long-lost unforgotten friend in Savoy, remembering how vainly he sought it through Paris, where cold Bacchus usurps the morning board, and how London, lost in smoke and steeped in tea, will not let a Yankee lisp the name. Canto II turns from praise to precept and to social comparison: the kitchen Muse framed her book to mix food by vicious rules of art, to sink the stomach and make friends wonder why children die, whereas the Yankee feast, furnished with simples and dressed with plainness, gathers a numerous offspring round the board and cheers servant and lord alike, health attending them from the short repast. The canto describes the morning cauldron, the mother stirring the pudding, the table spread and the bowls prepared, the children fed and combed and sent to school, and then, in the manner of an art of cookery, the exact rules of proportion and manipulation by which the purest of all foods may be made bad, indifferent or good. Canto III moves to the autumn: the days grow short, the corn-house is filled and the harvest home called, and the neighbours assemble for the corn-husking, a frolic scene where work, mirth and play chase the hours away among brown corn-fed nymphs and strong hard-handed beaux ranged in circling rows, the dry husks rustling and the corn-cobs cracking, cider tripping in silence round. The laws of husking are celebrated as the best-kept laws on earth - a kiss for every red ear, a bedaubing for the blackened ones, the favour'd beau who pays the luscious tribute - and the poem closes with mock-geometric precepts on the choice of spoons, the deep-bowl'd Gallic spoon being unfitted for substantial food, the true form being a small section of a goose-egg-shell, and the final advice not to fear to slaver but to suspend the ready napkin like the free Frenchman or poise the bowl upon the knee.
narrative_structure: Three cantos of continuous couplet argument, organised as a mock-epic and mock-didactic sequence rather than a story: invocation and praise in Canto I, social comparison and cookery precept in Canto II, harvest manners and the physiology of eating in Canto III. The single voice of the poet-speaker carries the poem, and its structure imitates the larger didactic epic it parodies, complete with a learned footnote of the author's own.
principal_characters: the exiled poet-speaker; the nameless Indian squaw, a tawny Ceres, who first invented the dish; Oella, the Peruvian heroine of the poet's earlier verse, to whom he alternatively ascribes the honour; the Yankee mother, the milk-maid and the children sent off to school; the brown corn-fed nymphs and strong hard-handed beaux of the husking; the free Frenchman with his napkin at his chin; the cook and the kitchen Muse of the vicious rules of art; the unnamed king of the note on proclamations against American principles
literary_form: Mock-heroic and verse satire in three cantos: a burlesque didactic poem on cookery and national diet built on the machinery of the epic invocation, the origin myth and the art-poem of precepts
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets throughout, closed decasyllabic pairs used for antithesis, sententious generalisation and the point of the joke ("Some tawny Ceres, goddess of her days, / First learn'd with stones to crack the well-dry'd maize"). The register shifts deliberately between epic solemnity, homely monosyllables of the cookery terms and mock-technical geometry, and the humour depends on the couplet's capacity to make a maxim out of a spoon. Barlow adds prose apparatus in the manner of the serious didactic poem, including the explanatory footnote on the king's proclamations.
historical_context: The poem was written in January 1793 at Chambéry in Savoy, in the year Barlow was travelling and writing on the continent as a republican sympathiser during the French Revolutionary wars, and its earliest printings appeared three years later, in 1796, when he was in Paris: a New Haven edition printed by T. and S. Green for Tiebout and O'Brien, a New York edition printed from the author's manuscript for Fellows and Adams, and a Poughkeepsie re-print, all in three cantos and all carrying the Chambéry date-line on the title page. The paratext of the Newburyport reprint of the companion poem The Conspiracy of Kings advertises its author on the title page as the author of Advice to the privileged orders, which places the pudding poem squarely in the same radical publishing campaign. Through the nineteenth century the poem remained in print, in editions of 1838, of 1847 printed with a memoir on maize or Indian corn by D. J. Browne, and of 1856, so that a Jacobin mock-heroic became a durable item of American domestic literary merchandise.
literary_significance: The Hasty-Pudding is the finest short American mock-heroic of the revolutionary decade and the one piece of Barlow's verse that has kept a continuous place in later anthologies and reprints. It matters for two reasons. As criticism it exposes, from inside, the conventions of the didactic and national epic that Barlow was himself attempting in the Columbiad material: the humble subject tests whether the machinery of invocation, origin myth and precept can be made to serve a republic of plain food rather than kings. As cultural argument it anticipates a persistent American theme, the moral contrast between European luxury and American plainness, and binds that contrast to a specific defence of indigenous and colonial material culture - the Indian inventor of maize cookery is named as the dish's true foundress, and the poem's English, French and Italian cityscapes are the places where the food cannot be found. Its footnote on royal proclamations against American principles also makes a cookery poem a document of the transatlantic radical publicity of 1792-1793.
attribution_notes: Single authorship is unproblematic: the 1796 editions print the poem by Joel Barlow and state the place and date of composition on the title page, one of them claiming to be printed from the author's manuscript. Bibliographical caution is needed rather than attributional caution, since several 1796 issues were printed from the same manuscript text in different cities and their title pages differ in detail - one reads Written in Germany, in Savoy, January, 1793 and others Written at Chambery, in Savoy - and the earliest surviving printed copy may not be the first appearance. This record's text and quotation are taken from the digitised 1796 New Haven edition in the Eighteenth-Century Poetry Archive (Evans text N22715), which is the source edition used by that archive.
bibliographical_notes: First printings, 1796: New Haven, printed by T. and S. Green for Tiebout and O'Brien(?), 8vo, 15, [1] pp. (the source edition of the Eighteenth-Century Poetry Archive text, Evans N22715); New York, printed from the author's manuscript for Fellows and Adams (Evans, listed in the Online Books Page Barlow enumeration); and a Poughkeepsie re-print by N. Power. Later editions include a New Haven printing of 1815 (Goodale and Burton), W. Storer, 1838, W. H. Graham, New York, 1847 (with D. J. Browne's Memoir on Maize or Indian Corn), and C. M. Saxton, 1856. Shaw and Shoemaker and the Evans Early American Imprint Transition database provide the bibliographical numbering for the 1796 issues.
